claims.claim: Muddy Waters moved to Chicago in 1943 and began electrifying his Delta blues guitar in 1944, a shift that became a foundation of Chicago electric blues.
claims.evidence: Britannica states Waters moved to Chicago in 1943 and began playing electric guitar in 1944.
claims.uncertainty: Exact year of electrification is a secondary-source simplification; Waters' Chicago arrival year is broadly corroborated across sources.

claims.claim: His Chicago bands included harmonica player Little Walter, guitarist Jimmy Rogers, and pianist Otis Spann, forming a core electric blues ensemble.
claims.evidence: Britannica lists Little Walter, Jimmy Rogers, and Otis Spann as collaborators in Waters' working bands.
claims.uncertainty: Band personnel varied across years; the named trio represents the classic mid-1950s lineup, not a fixed roster.

claims.claim: Waters recorded for Aristocrat and then Chess Records, placing him at the center of the Chess studio ecosystem in Chicago.
claims.evidence: Britannica records Waters' recording relationship with Aristocrat (which became Chess) and Chess Records.
claims.uncertainty: None material; label chronology is well documented.

claims.claim: Leonard Chess urged Howlin' Wolf to relocate to Chicago in 1952, making him a second pillar of the Chess blues roster alongside Muddy Waters.
claims.evidence: The Illinois Rock & Roll Museum on Route 66 states Leonard Chess urged Burnett to move to Chicago in 1952.
claims.source: Illinois Rock & Roll Museum on Route 66 (https://roadtorock.org/artist/chester-burnett-aka-howlin-wolf/)
claims.uncertainty: The museum is a regional institution; the 1952 move is corroborated across blues histories.

claims.claim: His Chicago bands featured guitarist Hubert Sumlin and other leading players of the Chicago blues scene.
claims.evidence: The Illinois Rock & Roll Museum notes his bands included Hubert Sumlin and other major Chicago players.
claims.source: Illinois Rock & Roll Museum on Route 66 (https://roadtorock.org/artist/chester-burnett-aka-howlin-wolf/)
claims.uncertainty: Source names Sumlin without full personnel detail; Sumlin's long association with Wolf is broadly corroborated.

claims.claim: Willie Dixon worked as a songwriter, arranger, producer, and bassist, serving as a connective studio node across the Chess blues roster.
claims.evidence: American Music Pioneers describes Dixon's combined roles as songwriter, arranger, producer, and bassist.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; the multi-role description is widely repeated in blues literature but should be corroborated.

claims.claim: Dixon wrote for and worked with Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Little Walter, and Koko Taylor, linking generations of Chicago blues artists.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on the relationships themselves.
claims.evidence: American Music Pioneers connects Dixon's writing and studio work to Waters, Wolf, Little Walter, and Taylor.
claims.uncertainty: Individual song attributions (e.g., authorship shares on specific titles) carry their own disputes not adjudicated here.

claims.claim: Dixon served as talent scout, producer, arranger, songwriter, and bassist for the Cobra Records generation of Otis Rush, Magic Sam, and Buddy Guy.
claims.evidence: Cobra Records history and PRX oral-history material describe Dixon's multi-role work with Rush, Magic Sam, and Guy at Cobra.
claims.source: Cobra Records history (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_Records); PRX exchange piece (http://exchange.prx.org/pieces/446963?m=false)
claims.uncertainty: PRX piece is oral-history-derived; Cobra's catalog history is documented but thin on primary sources.

claims.claim: Koko Taylor moved to Chicago, was discovered by Willie Dixon, and built her career through a relationship with Chess Records.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (Extension of Remarks, vol. 150) and NPR-derived reporting describe her Chicago move, Dixon's discovery, and Chess association.
claims.uncertainty: The Congressional tribute is a memorial document; factual claims are corroborated by obituary reporting.

claims.claim: Her recording 'Wang Dang Doodle' sold a million copies, establishing her as the leading woman of Chicago electric blues in the 1960s.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute and NPR obituary reporting cite the million-selling 'Wang Dang Doodle'.
claims.uncertainty: Million-copy figure comes from a memorial tribute; sales accounting from the era is imprecise.

claims.claim: Buddy Guy moved to Chicago in 1957 and did session work for Chess Records, with Willie Dixon acting as a mentor.
claims.evidence: The Ford music database and LA Sentinel reporting describe his 1957 Chicago arrival, Chess session work, and Dixon's mentorship.
claims.source: The Ford music database (https://www.theford.com/musicdb/artists/2215/buddy-guy); LA Sentinel (https://lasentinel.net/buddy-guy-looks-to-the-future-of-the-blues.html)
claims.uncertainty: Mentorship framing is interpretive; Dixon's producer role at Guy's early sessions is documented.

claims.claim: Guy collaborated with harmonica player Junior Wells, forming one of the signature Chicago blues partnerships.
claims.evidence: LA Sentinel reporting documents the Guy–Wells collaboration.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source for the specific partnership framing; the collaboration itself is widely documented.

claims.claim: Little Walter played in Muddy Waters' band and pioneered amplified harmonica technique in Chicago.
claims.evidence: All About Jazz describes his Waters band membership and amplified-harmonica innovation.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; both the band role and the amplification innovation are widely repeated in blues histories.

claims.claim: His 1952 instrumental 'Juke' was a major hit, the first harmonica instrumental to top the R&B charts.
claims.evidence: All About Jazz cites the 1952 'Juke' hit.
claims.uncertainty: 'First harmonica instrumental to top the charts' is a common claim needing a chart-data source.

claims.claim: The exact year of Little Walter's Chicago arrival is uncertain: sources give 1945, 1946, or 1947.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The competing years 1945, 1946, and 1947 appear across secondary sources.
claims.evidence: Secondary biographies conflict across the three years.
claims.source: Multiple secondary biographies; see All About Jazz (http://www.allaboutjazz.com/musicians/little-walter)
claims.uncertainty: No primary record located to resolve the arrival year.

claims.claim: Otis Rush was part of the new West Side generation recorded by Cobra Records, with Willie Dixon as talent scout, producer, arranger, songwriter, and bassist.
claims.evidence: Cobra Records history and PRX oral-history material place Rush in the Cobra generation with Dixon's multi-role involvement.
claims.source: Cobra Records history (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobra_Records); PRX exchange piece (http://exchange.prx.org/pieces/446963?m=false)
claims.uncertainty: Oral-history-derived; Cobra's catalog and Dixon's roles are documented but primary session records are thin.

claims.claim: Rush's Cobra recordings helped define the West Side blues sound distinct from the South Side Chess sound.
claims.evidence: Cobra Records history frames Rush, Magic Sam, and Buddy Guy as a West Side generation.
claims.uncertainty: The South Side/West Side sonic distinction is a critical framing, not a documented artist claim.

claims.claim: Magic Sam was part of the Cobra Records West Side generation alongside Otis Rush and Buddy Guy, with Willie Dixon in production and songwriting roles.
claims.evidence: Cobra Records history groups Magic Sam with Rush and Guy as Dixon-produced Cobra artists.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source grouping; individual session credits need primary documentation.

claims.claim: His later Delmark recordings, including 'West Side Soul' (1967), extended the West Side sound beyond Cobra's collapse.
claims.evidence: Discographic record of the 1967 Delmark album 'West Side Soul' is widely cited; Cobra collapsed in 1959.
claims.source: General discographic record (no single URL verified in this pass)
claims.uncertainty: No source was pulled for this claim in this research pass; album title and year need verification.

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey moved to Chicago in 1919 and led music at Pilgrim Baptist Church, becoming the central architect of modern gospel music.
claims.evidence: Plaque transcription and LA Sentinel reporting describe his 1919 Chicago move and Pilgrim Baptist leadership.
claims.uncertainty: The 'father of gospel' title is honorific; Dorsey's Chicago role is corroborated across sources.

claims.claim: Dorsey authored 'Take My Hand, Precious Lord' and built gospel's publishing and convention infrastructure.
claims.evidence: LA Sentinel reporting cites the song and his publishing/convention work.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: One plaque transcription for Dorsey contains an impossible 'August 36' date for his wife's death and must not be reproduced as fact.
claims.evidence: The plaque transcription itself contains the impossible date.
claims.uncertainty: The plaque text is a transcription artifact; Dorsey's wife Nettie died in childbirth in 1932 per standard biographies.

claims.claim: Mahalia Jackson moved to Chicago in 1927 and worked with Thomas A. Dorsey, anchoring the Chicago gospel tradition.
claims.evidence: Biographical sources describe her 1927 Chicago move and work with Dorsey.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source in this pass; the Dorsey–Jackson association is widely corroborated.

claims.claim: Her 1947 recording 'Move On Up a Little Higher' was a landmark gospel success, but reported sales totals conflict: one million, two million, and eight million copies are all claimed.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Sources variously claim one million, two million, and eight million copies sold.
claims.evidence: Recording history (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Move_On_Up_a_Little_Higher) documents the 1947 release; sales figures vary across secondary sources.
claims.uncertainty: The recording's success is verified; the exact sales total cannot be resolved from available sources.

claims.claim: Sallie Martin worked as a performer, promoter, and business strategist in Chicago gospel, co-founding Martin & Morris Publishing.
claims.evidence: Baylor/KWBU 'Shout' material emphasizes her performer, promoter, and business roles and the publishing company.
claims.source: KWBU / Baylor 'Shout: Black Gospel Music Moments' (https://www.kwbu.org/show/shout-black-gospel-music-moments/2022-11-27/shout-black-gospel-music-moments-sallie-martin)
claims.uncertainty: Single program source; her business role is increasingly recognized in gospel scholarship but needs archival corroboration.

claims.claim: Martin's Sallie Martin Gospel Singers included a young Dinah Washington (then Ruth Jones) as a lead vocalist.
claims.evidence: Dinah Washington biographical material (Last.fm, citing standard biographies) states she sang with the Sallie Martin Gospel Singers.
claims.uncertainty: Secondary sourcing; the Washington–Martin link is a standard biographical claim.

claims.claim: Roberta Martin was guided by Thomas A. Dorsey and Theodore Frye; the Martin-Frye Quartet formed in 1933 and evolved into the Roberta Martin Singers in 1936.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian archival description documents Dorsey and Frye's guidance and the 1933/1936 group evolution.
claims.uncertainty: Archival finding aid; dates are collection-level descriptions.

claims.claim: Albertina Walker was born in Chicago in 1929, sang in West Point Baptist Church's youth choir, and was mentored by Mahalia Jackson, who took her on the road as a teenager.
claims.evidence: NEA National Heritage Fellowship page and Wikipedia document her Chicago birth, West Point choir, and Jackson mentorship.
claims.uncertainty: The NEA page is an authoritative federal source; details corroborated across obituaries.

claims.claim: In 1951 she organized the Caravans, which launched the careers of Shirley Caesar, Inez Andrews, Dorothy Norwood, and James Cleveland, earning her the 'Star Maker' nickname.
claims.evidence: NEA page states she organized the Caravans at age 22 and lists the launched careers; African American Registry confirms the 'Star Maker' nickname.
claims.uncertainty: NEA is authoritative; the roster of launched careers is corroborated.

claims.claim: She was popularly called the 'Queen of Gospel Music' after Mahalia Jackson's death in 1972, won the 1995 Grammy for Best Traditional Gospel Album, and received ten Grammy nominations.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and NEA document the title, the 1995 Grammy win, and ten nominations.
claims.uncertainty: The 'Queen of Gospel Music' title is honorific, initially bestowed by Rev. James Cleveland and Rev. Jesse Jackson per Wikipedia.

claims.claim: The Caravans were founded by Albertina Walker in 1951 from members of the Robert Anderson Singers, becoming one of the most prominent gospel groups of the 1950s–60s.
claims.evidence: Hymnary and NEA document the 1951 founding from Robert Anderson Singers members.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The group's fluctuating membership included James Cleveland, Bessie Griffin, Shirley Caesar, Dorothy Norwood, Inez Andrews, Loleatta Holloway, and Cassietta George.
claims.evidence: African American Registry and Hymnary list the rotating membership.
claims.uncertainty: Membership lists vary across sources; the core names are consistent.

claims.claim: King Oliver moved to Chicago in 1919, founded his Creole Jazz Band, and in 1922 sent for his protégé Louis Armstrong to join him.
claims.evidence: Old Time Blues documents the 1919 Chicago move, the Creole Jazz Band, and the 1922 summons of Armstrong.
claims.uncertainty: Single enthusiast source; the 1919/1922 chronology is standard in jazz histories.

claims.claim: Oliver's Creole Jazz Band made its first records for Gennett in Richmond, Indiana, on April 5, 1923 — among the first important recordings by Black jazz musicians.
claims.evidence: Old Time Blues records the April 5, 1923 Gennett session and subsequent Okeh, Columbia, and Paramount sides.
claims.uncertainty: 'First important' is an interpretive ranking; the session date is well documented.

claims.claim: In 1922 Armstrong followed his mentor Joe 'King' Oliver to Chicago to play second cornet in the Creole Jazz Band.
claims.evidence: Multiple biographical sources document the 1922 Chicago move at Oliver's invitation.
claims.source: Making Music Fun biography (https://makingmusicfun.net/public/assets/pdf/printit-biographies/louis-armstrong-printit-biography.pdf); Scribd biography summary
claims.uncertainty: None material; the 1922 move is one of the best-documented facts in jazz history.

claims.claim: After leaving Oliver, Armstrong returned to Chicago in 1925, playing with his wife Lil Hardin's band at the Dreamland Café and recording the Hot Five/Hot Seven sessions.
claims.evidence: Armstrong biographies document the 1925 return and Dreamland Café engagement with Lil Hardin's band.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source in this pass; the Hot Five sessions are documented Chicago recordings of 1925–28.

claims.claim: Lil Hardin was the pianist and arranger of King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band in Chicago and married Louis Armstrong in 1924.
claims.evidence: Armstrong biographies list Hardin as the Creole Jazz Band's pianist and note the 1924 marriage.
claims.source: PicoBlog Armstrong biography (https://gregoden.s3.uk.io.cloud.ovh.net/louis-armstrong-biography-jazz-musician-satchmo.html); YouTube Gennett session notes
claims.uncertainty: Secondary sourcing; her arranger role is documented in jazz histories.

claims.claim: Hardin pushed Armstrong to leave Oliver's band and join Fletcher Henderson in New York, and later led her own band at Chicago's Dreamland Café.
claims.evidence: PicoBlog biography describes her urging the Henderson move and her Dreamland Café band.
claims.uncertainty: The narrative of her influence on the career move is standard but interpretive.

claims.claim: Earl Hines moved to Chicago in 1925, met Louis Armstrong at the Musicians' Union, and on December 28, 1928 opened at the Grand Terrace Café leading his own big band.
claims.evidence: TheBlues-ThatJazz biography documents the 1925 move, the Armstrong meeting, and the December 28, 1928 Grand Terrace opening.
claims.uncertainty: Enthusiast source; the Grand Terrace opening date is widely corroborated.

claims.claim: Hines' Grand Terrace orchestra became one of the most broadcast Black bands in America, and his band nurtured musicians including Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Billy Eckstine.
claims.evidence: Sonichits and Penn State Center for the Book document the broadcasts and the Gillespie/Parker/Eckstine connections.
claims.source: Sonichits (https://sonichits.com/album/Earl_Hines/Complete_Jazz_Series_1937_-_1939); PA Center for the Book (http://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/bios/hines__earl_fatha)
claims.uncertainty: 'Most broadcast band in America' is an enthusiast claim needing broadcast-log verification; the sideman careers are documented.

claims.claim: Nat 'King' Cole sometimes served as Hines' relief pianist at the Grand Terrace.
claims.evidence: Sonichits notes Cole as an occasional relief pianist for Hines.
claims.uncertainty: Single enthusiast source; the Hines-to-Cole influence is well documented but the relief-pianist detail needs corroboration.

claims.claim: Nat King Cole was born in Montgomery, Alabama, and raised in Chicago, where his biggest early influence was Earl Hines.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Birth year given as 1917 (Donald Clarke) vs 1919 (NPR).
claims.evidence: NPR (via KMUC/WCMU) documents the Montgomery birth, Chicago upbringing, and Hines influence; Donald Clarke's encyclopedia corroborates.
claims.source: NPR via KMUC (https://www.kmuc.org/2019-03-17/nat-king-cole-still-remains-one-of-the-great-gifts-of-nature-100-years-later); Donald Clarke Music Box (http://www.donaldclarkemusicbox.com/encyclopedia/detail.php?s=694)
claims.uncertainty: NPR gives birth year 1919; most references give 1917 (some 1919). Birth year is disputed and not adjudicated here.

claims.claim: Cole formed the King Cole Trio in 1939 with guitar, bass, and piano — a format that influenced Oscar Peterson and Ahmad Jamal.
claims.evidence: Donald Clarke's encyclopedia documents the 1939 trio formation; NPR notes the influence on Peterson and Jamal.
claims.source: Donald Clarke Music Box (http://www.donaldclarkemusicbox.com/encyclopedia/detail.php?s=694); NPR via KMUC (https://www.kmuc.org/2019-03-17/nat-king-cole-still-remains-one-of-the-great-gifts-of-nature-100-years-later)
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Cole studied at Chicago's DuSable High School music program before leaving as a teenager to become a professional musician.
claims.evidence: Legacy.com's fact list documents DuSable High School participation.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; DuSable attendance is standard in Cole biographies.

claims.claim: Ahmad Jamal broke through with his small-group music in Chicago in the 1950s; his trio became the house band at the Pershing Hotel in 1958.
claims.evidence: NPR Fresh Air (Kevin Whitehead) documents the Chicago breakthrough and Pershing Hotel residency; WWFM Piano Jazz corroborates.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The 1958 Pershing Hotel live album 'But Not for Me' yielded his hit 'Poinciana', which stayed on the charts for over two years and was a financial lifesaver for Chess's Argo subsidiary.
claims.evidence: NPR Fresh Air and WWFM document the album, 'Poinciana', chart run, and Argo/Chess connection.
claims.uncertainty: 'Lifesaver for Argo' is Whitehead's characterization; the album's commercial success is documented.

claims.claim: Miles Davis testified to Jamal's influence on his own use of space, silence, and formal variation.
claims.evidence: NPR Fresh Air quotes Davis's acknowledged influence.
claims.uncertainty: Davis's statements about Jamal are documented in interviews; the specific musical borrowings are critical interpretation.

claims.claim: Ramsey Lewis was born in Chicago in 1935, grew up in the Cabrini-Green Homes, and formed the Ramsey Lewis Trio with Redd Holt and Eldee Young, signing to Chess Records.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia documents the Chicago birth, Cabrini-Green upbringing, trio formation, and Chess signing; soulwalking corroborates.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The trio's 1965 'The In Crowd' reached No. 5 on the pop charts and No. 2 on the album chart, crossing jazz into the pop mainstream.
claims.evidence: Soulwalking and Popdose document the 1965 chart performance.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Drummer Maurice White played in the Ramsey Lewis Trio before leaving to form Earth, Wind & Fire, linking Chicago jazz directly to Chicago funk.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia and soulwalking document White's trio tenure and departure to form Earth, Wind & Fire.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Dinah Washington was born in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, moved to Chicago at age three, and sang gospel in church before entering secular music.
claims.evidence: AllMusic and Rhino document the Chicago move, church gospel background, and Ruth Jones name.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: She won a talent contest at the Regal Theater, played Chicago's Garrick Stage Bar, joined Lionel Hampton, and made her recording debut for Keynote Records in late 1943.
claims.evidence: AllMusic documents the Regal contest, Garrick Stage Bar, Hampton band, and Keynote debut.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: As a young singer she worked with the Sallie Martin Gospel Singers, tying her directly to the Chicago gospel lineage.
claims.evidence: Last.fm biography (citing standard biographies) states she sang with the Sallie Martin Gospel Singers.
claims.uncertainty: Secondary sourcing; consistent across biographies.

claims.claim: Von Freeman was born in Chicago, learned under Walter Dyett at DuSable High School, worked at the Pershing Hotel, and associated with Sun Ra.
claims.evidence: Selmer artist page documents the Chicago birth, Dyett training, Pershing work, and Sun Ra association.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: He led South Side jazz jam sessions for more than 40 years and became the central figure of Chicago's hard-bop tenor school.
claims.evidence: Selmer documents the four-decade jam-session leadership; the tenor-school characterization is critical consensus.
claims.uncertainty: 'Father of Chicago jazz' framings are honorific.

claims.claim: Johnny Griffin grew up in Chicago, studied at DuSable High School, played with Lionel Hampton, and became a leading hard-bop tenor saxophonist.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia documents the Chicago upbringing, DuSable study, Hampton tenure, and hard-bop career.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source in this pass; details are standard in jazz reference works.

claims.claim: Griffin was part of the Chicago tenor lineage alongside Von Freeman, representing the city's hard-bop saxophone school.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia documents his Chicago origins and hard-bop tenor career.
claims.uncertainty: The 'lineage' framing is interpretive, not a documented relationship.

claims.claim: Sun Ra moved to Chicago in January 1946, worked with Fletcher Henderson, and developed his Arkestra and Afrofuturist practice during his Chicago years.
claims.evidence: All About Jazz and Spectrum Culture document the January 1946 move, Henderson work, and Chicago-era Arkestra development.
claims.uncertainty: The 'Afrofuturist practice' framing is scholarly; his Chicago-era experimentation is documented.

claims.claim: His Chicago period included residencies and community work on the South Side that shaped the Arkestra's communal, multidisciplinary model.
claims.evidence: Spectrum Culture documents his South Side Chicago period and communal practice.
claims.uncertainty: Details of specific residencies need archival corroboration.

claims.claim: Muhal Richard Abrams co-founded the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians (AACM) in 1965 and served as its first president.
claims.evidence: Jazz88 and Pi Recordings document the 1965 founding and his first presidency.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: His 1967 album 'Levels and Degrees of Light' was an early landmark of the AACM recording era.
claims.evidence: Jazz88 documents the 1967 album's landmark status.
claims.uncertainty: 'Landmark' is critical framing.

claims.claim: Abrams worked in Chicago blues, R&B, and hard-bop before the AACM, tying the avant-garde to the city's Black popular-music lineage.
claims.evidence: Pi Recordings documents his pre-AACM Chicago blues/R&B/hard-bop work.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Nicole Mitchell moved to Chicago around 1990, joined the AACM in 1994, and became the organization's first woman president.
claims.evidence: AACM's own site documents her Chicago arrival, 1994 membership, and first-woman-president role.
claims.uncertainty: Black Earth Ensemble founding year is given as 1997 or 1998 across sources; the AACM details are from the organization's own site.

claims.claim: She founded the Black Earth Ensemble, extending the AACM tradition through a Black feminist compositional practice.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Founding year given as 1997 in some sources, 1998 in others.
claims.evidence: AACM site and biographies document the ensemble's founding.
claims.uncertainty: Exact founding year is provisional pending resolution of the 1997/1998 conflict.

claims.claim: Makaya McCraven moved to Chicago in 2007 and developed a live-improvisation-and-editing method through the 52-week 'In the Moment' residency series.
claims.evidence: Earshot Jazz documents the 2007 move and the 'In the Moment' series method.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: His 2018 album 'Universal Beings' linked Chicago players — including cellist Tomeka Reid — with London and New York improvisers, positioning Chicago in a global contemporary jazz network.
claims.evidence: Flying Out and Earshot document the album's cross-city sessions and Reid's participation.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Tomeka Reid is a Chicago-based cellist and composer active in the AACM orbit, appearing on Makaya McCraven's 'Universal Beings' (2018).
claims.evidence: Flying Out credits Reid's cello on 'Universal Beings'.
claims.uncertainty: Single source in this pass; Reid's AACM leadership roles need direct sourcing.

claims.claim: Reid's quartet and string work extend the AACM string tradition into contemporary Chicago creative music.
claims.evidence: General critical coverage of Reid's quartet exists but was not pulled in this pass.
claims.uncertainty: No source pulled for this claim; needs direct evidence.

claims.claim: The Art Ensemble of Chicago formed in 1969 from AACM members, carrying the organization's 'Great Black Music' concept to international stages.
claims.evidence: AllMusic's Abrams biography and general reference works document the 1969 formation from AACM membership.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source in this pass; the 1969 formation is standard in jazz histories.

claims.claim: The group's multidisciplinary performances — costumes, poetry, theater — made it the AACM's most visible ambassador.
claims.evidence: Critical consensus documented across jazz histories; no single source pulled in this pass.
claims.uncertainty: No source pulled; needs direct evidence.

claims.claim: Sam Cooke was born in Clarksdale, Mississippi, moved with his family to Chicago in 1933, and grew up in the Bronzeville neighborhood.
claims.contradictory_evidence: One search-result snippet incorrectly identified Chicago as his birthplace; stronger accounts give Clarksdale, Mississippi.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com and EBSCO document the Clarksdale birth and 1933 family migration to Chicago.
claims.uncertainty: Birthplace resolved as Clarksdale; the Chicago-birth snippet is rejected as erroneous.

claims.claim: Cooke sang with the Highway QCs and then the Soul Stirrers before his gospel-to-secular crossover as a solo soul artist.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com documents the Highway QCs and Soul Stirrers tenures.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Curtis Mayfield formed the Impressions with Jerry Butler, writing and singing on hits including 'People Get Ready'.
claims.evidence: Britannica documents the Butler partnership, the Impressions, and 'People Get Ready'.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: He left the Impressions in 1970 for a solo career and scored the 1972 film 'Super Fly', whose soundtrack became a landmark of socially conscious funk-soul.
claims.evidence: Britannica documents the 1970 departure and the 'Super Fly' soundtrack.
claims.uncertainty: 'Landmark' is critical consensus.

claims.claim: Through his Curtom label and songwriting for Chicago artists, Mayfield anchored the city's independent soul infrastructure.
claims.evidence: Britannica documents the Curtom label; soulwalking documents his songwriting for Gene Chandler and Major Lance.
claims.uncertainty: 'Anchored the infrastructure' is interpretive; Curtom's role is documented.

claims.claim: Jerry Butler was Curtis Mayfield's partner in the Impressions and a solo soul star, with Chicago roots in the church vocal tradition.
claims.evidence: Britannica's Mayfield biography documents the Butler–Mayfield Impressions partnership; soulwalking documents Butler's Chicago career.
claims.uncertainty: Soulwalking entry exists but was not fully read in this pass; treat solo-career details as provisional.

claims.claim: Butler's circle connected Mayfield to Major Lance and other Chicago soul artists, making him a node in the 1960s Chicago soul network.
claims.evidence: The Major Lance biography (tsimon.com) documents the Butler–Mayfield–Lance social ties.
claims.uncertainty: 'Node in the network' is interpretive; the personal ties are documented.

claims.claim: Mavis Staples sang lead for the Staple Singers, the Chicago family group that moved from gospel to message-driven soul hits at Stax.
claims.evidence: Masters of Traditional Arts documents the Chicago family group and the gospel-to-soul movement; Louder Sound corroborates.
claims.source: Masters of Traditional Arts (http://www.mastersoftraditionalarts.org/artists/312?selected_facets=); Louder Sound (https://www.loudersound.com/features/mavis-staples-the-life-and-soul-of-a-legend)
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Staples later collaborated with Curtis Mayfield, extending the Chicago gospel-soul lineage into the 1970s and beyond.
claims.evidence: Louder Sound documents the Mayfield collaboration.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source in this pass.

claims.claim: The Staple Singers were a Chicago family gospel group led by Roebuck 'Pops' Staples that became hitmakers at Stax with message songs like 'Respect Yourself' and 'I'll Take You There'.
claims.evidence: Masters of Traditional Arts documents the Chicago family formation and the Stax message-song era.
claims.uncertainty: Song titles are standard discographic facts.

claims.claim: Mavis Staples' lead vocals carried the group's sound from church to the pop charts without abandoning its gospel identity.
claims.evidence: Louder Sound documents Staples' central vocal role and the gospel-retention framing.
claims.uncertainty: Interpretive framing.

claims.claim: Gene Chandler grew up on Chicago's South Side, sang with the Dukays, and hit No. 1 in 1962 with 'Duke of Earl'.
claims.evidence: Soulwalking documents the South Side roots, the Dukays, and the 'Duke of Earl' No. 1.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Chandler later recorded Curtis Mayfield-written material, tying the Chicago doo-wop generation to Mayfield's soul era.
claims.evidence: Soulwalking documents the Mayfield-written recordings.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source.

claims.claim: Major Lance moved to Chicago as a child, befriended Curtis Mayfield and Jerry Butler, and became an Okeh Records star with Mayfield-written hits like 'The Monkey Time' and 'Um, Um, Um, Um, Um, Um'.
claims.evidence: Tsimon.com and soulwalking document the childhood move, the Mayfield/Butler ties, Okeh tenure, and Mayfield-written hits.
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: The Chi-Lites formed in Chicago, with Eugene Record as lead singer, songwriter, and producer; Record co-wrote Barbara Acklin's hits and the group's own 'Have You Seen Her' and 'Oh Girl'.
claims.evidence: AllMusic documents the Chicago formation and Record's triple role; the Acklin co-writing and hit titles are documented.
